summary.text: The proof takes \(K=((3(2r+1))!)^r\) and compares prime-adic valuations using Legendre’s formula. Contributions up to \(v_p((3(2r+1))!)\) are absorbed by \(K\); for every larger \(p^i\) dividing a factor, the congruence \(8n\equiv 2k+1\pmod{p^i}\) yields a floor-function contribution of at least one to the valuation of the factorial ratio, and size bounds ensure that such a large prime power divides at most one factor.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\frac{(8n)!\,n!}{(4n)!(3n)!(2n)!}
\qquad(n\ge 0).
\]
For fixed \(r\ge 0\), put
\[
D_r(n)=\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}\bigl(8n-(2k+1)\bigr).
\]
We shall prove that one may take the explicit positive integer
\[
K(r)=\left(\bigl(3(2r+1)\bigr)!\right)^r.
\]
Thus the assertion will follow once we prove
\[
D_r(n)\mid K(r)a(n)
\]
in \(\mathbb Z\) for every \(n\ge 0\).

We use \(v_p(m)\) for the exponent of a prime \(p\) in a nonzero positive integer \(m\).

## 1. Two floor inequalities

The proof rests on two elementary inequalities involving floors.

### The basic inequality

For all nonnegative integers \(n\) and all positive integers \(q\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{4n}{q}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3n}{q}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{q}\right\rfloor
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{8n}{q}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac n q\right\rfloor.
\tag{1}
\]

To prove this, write \(n=uq+c\), where \(0\le c<q\). The contributions involving \(u\) on the two sides are both \(9u\), so it is enough to prove
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{4c}{q}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3c}{q}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{2c}{q}\right\rfloor
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{8c}{q}\right\rfloor.
\tag{2}
\]
Let
\[
j=\left\lfloor\frac{8c}{q}\right\rfloor.
\]
Since \(c<q\), we have \(j\in\{0,1,\ldots,7\}\). The eight cases follow directly from
\(jq\le 8c<(j+1)q\). More explicitly, upper bounds for the three floors on the left of (2), in the order \(4c,3c,2c\), are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
j&
\bigl(\lfloor4c/q\rfloor,\lfloor3c/q\rfloor,\lfloor2c/q\rfloor\bigr)
\text{ is at most}&\text{sum}\cr
\hline
0&(0,0,0)&0\cr
1&(0,0,0)&0\cr
2&(1,1,0)&2\cr
3&(1,1,0)&2\cr
4&(2,1,1)&4\cr
5&(2,2,1)&5\cr
6&(3,2,1)&6\cr
7&(3,2,1)&6.
\end{array}
\]
Every displayed sum is at most \(j\), proving (2), and hence (1).

### A strengthened inequality

We shall also need the following stronger statement. Suppose that \(q,s\) are positive odd integers, \(3s<q\), and
\[
8n\equiv s\pmod q.
\tag{3}
\]
Then
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{4n}{q}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3n}{q}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{q}\right\rfloor+1
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{8n}{q}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac n q\right\rfloor.
\tag{4}
\]

Again write \(n=uq+c\), with \(0\le c<q\). As before, the terms involving \(u\) cancel. Congruence (3), together with \(0<s<q\), says precisely that
\[
8c=jq+s,
\qquad j=\left\lfloor\frac{8c}{q}\right\rfloor\in\{0,1,\ldots,7\}.
\tag{5}
\]
Because \(8c\) is even while \(q\) and \(s\) are odd, (5) implies that \(j\) is odd. Thus only \(j=1,3,5,7\) can occur.

We check these four cases.

* If \(j=1\), then \(8c=q+s<\frac43q\), because \(3s<q\). Hence \(4c,3c,2c<q\). The three floors are all zero, so their sum plus \(1\) is \(1=j\).

* If \(j=3\), then \(8c=3q+s<\frac{10}{3}q\). It follows that
  \[
  4c<2q,\qquad 3c<2q,\qquad 2c<q.
  \]
  Thus the three floors are at most \(1,1,0\), and their sum plus \(1\) is at most \(3=j\).

* If \(j=5\), then \(8c=5q+s<\frac{16}{3}q\). Consequently
  \[
  4c<3q,\qquad 3c<2q,\qquad 2c<2q.
  \]
  The floors are therefore at most \(2,1,1\), and their sum plus \(1\) is at most \(5=j\).

* If \(j=7\), the simple bound \(c<q\) gives
  \[
  \left\lfloor\frac{4c}{q}\right\rfloor\le3,
  \quad
  \left\lfloor\frac{3c}{q}\right\rfloor\le2,
  \quad
  \left\lfloor\frac{2c}{q}\right\rfloor\le1.
  \]
  Their sum plus \(1\) is at most \(7=j\).

This proves (4).

## 2. Integrality and the prime valuations of \(a(n)\)

Legendre’s formula gives, for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_p(m!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor,
\tag{6}
\]
where only finitely many terms are nonzero. Applying (1) with \(q=p^i\), and summing over \(i\ge1\), yields
\[
v_p((4n)!)+v_p((3n)!)+v_p((2n)!)
\le v_p((8n)!)+v_p(n!).
\]
This holds for every prime \(p\), so
\[
(4n)!(3n)!(2n)!\mid (8n)!n!.
\]
In particular, \(a(n)\) is a positive integer.

For later use, define
\[
F_{p,i}(n)=
\left\lfloor\frac{8n}{p^i}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac n{p^i}\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor\frac{4n}{p^i}\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor\frac{3n}{p^i}\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{7}
\]
By (1), each \(F_{p,i}(n)\) is nonnegative. Legendre’s formula gives the exact identity
\[
v_p(a(n))=\sum_{i\ge1}F_{p,i}(n).
\tag{8}
\]
The sum is finite: all terms vanish once \(p^i>8n\).

## 3. A large prime power dividing one linear factor contributes to \(a(n)\)

For \(k\ge0\), set
\[
s_k=2k+1,
\qquad
d_k(n)=|8n-s_k|.
\]
Notice that \(d_k(n)\ne0\), because \(8n\) is even and \(s_k\) is odd. Moreover, \(d_k(n)\) is odd.

We claim that if \(p\) is prime and
\[
p^i\mid d_k(n),
\qquad p^i>3s_k,
\tag{9}
\]
then
\[
F_{p,i}(n)\ge1.
\tag{10}
\]
Indeed, because \(p^i\) divides the odd number \(d_k(n)\), the number \(p^i\) is odd. Divisibility in (9) implies
\[
8n\equiv s_k\pmod {p^i}.
\]
Also \(3s_k<p^i\), so in particular \(0<s_k<p^i\). We may therefore apply the strengthened floor inequality (4) with \(q=p^i\) and \(s=s_k\). It gives exactly (10).

We also record why every prime power to which we apply this observation occurs within the finite range of the sum (8). Suppose
\[
p^i\mid d_k(n),\qquad p^i>s_k.
\tag{11}
\]
Then \(p^i\le 8n\). To see this, if \(8n\ge s_k\), then
\[
d_k(n)=8n-s_k,
\]
and, since a positive divisor of a positive integer is no larger than that integer,
\(p^i\le d_k(n)\le8n\). On the other hand, if \(8n<s_k\), then
\[
0<d_k(n)=s_k-8n<s_k<p^i,
\]
which is impossible if \(p^i\mid d_k(n)\). Hence the second case cannot occur. Thus (11) indeed implies \(p^i\le8n\).

## 4. Choice of the constant and separation of small and large exponents

Fix \(r\ge0\), and put
\[
M=3(2r+1),
\qquad C=M!,
\qquad K=C^r.
\tag{12}
\]
We prove, prime by prime, that
\[
\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}d_k(n)\mid a(n)K.
\tag{13}
\]

Fix a prime \(p\), and write
\[
e_k=v_p(d_k(n))\quad(0\le k<r),
\qquad t=v_p(C)=v_p(M!).
\tag{14}
\]
The \(p\)-adic valuation of the left side of (13) is \(\sum_{k<r}e_k\), while
\[
v_p(K)=rt.
\tag{15}
\]
The first \(t\) copies of \(p\) in each \(d_k(n)\) can therefore be paid for by \(K\). It remains to show that all exponents beyond \(t\) can be paid for by \(a(n)\).

Consider the set of pairs
\[
\mathcal S=\{(k,i):0\le k<r,\ t<i\le e_k\}.
\tag{16}
\]
For every \((k,i)\in\mathcal S\), we have \(p^i\mid d_k(n)\). Furthermore, since \(i>v_p(M!)\), the prime power \(p^i\) does not divide \(M!\). This forces
\[
p^i>M.
\tag{17}
\]
Indeed, if \(p^i\le M\), then \(p^i\), being one of the positive integers at most \(M\), would divide \(M!\), a contradiction.

Because \(k<r\), we have
\[
3s_k=3(2k+1)<3(2r+1)=M<p^i.
\]
Thus the result of Section 3 applies and gives
\[
F_{p,i}(n)\ge1
\qquad\text{for every }(k,i)\in\mathcal S.
\tag{18}
\]
It also gives \(p^i\le8n\), so these \(i\)'s lie among the indices that can occur in (8).

The crucial point is that the second-coordinate map
\[
(k,i)\longmapsto i
\]
is injective on \(\mathcal S\). Suppose that both \((k,i)\) and \((\ell,i)\) belong to \(\mathcal S\). Then \(p^i\) divides both
\[
8n-(2k+1)\quad\text{and}\quad8n-(2\ell+1)
\]
in absolute value, and hence it divides their difference
\[
(2\ell+1)-(2k+1)=2(\ell-k).
\]
If \(k\ne\ell\), the absolute value of this nonzero difference is less than \(2r\), and therefore certainly less than
\[
M=3(2r+1)<p^i.
\]
A positive integer cannot divide a nonzero integer of smaller absolute value. Hence \(k=\ell\), proving injectivity.

It follows from (18), injectivity, and (8) that
\[
|\mathcal S|
\le \sum_{i\ge1}F_{p,i}(n)
=v_p(a(n)).
\tag{19}
\]
But by its definition,
\[
|\mathcal S|=\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}\max(e_k-t,0).
\tag{20}
\]
For every \(k\),
\[
e_k\le t+\max(e_k-t,0).
\]
Summing and using (19) gives
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}e_k
\le rt+|\mathcal S|
\le rt+v_p(a(n))
=v_p(K)+v_p(a(n)).
\tag{21}
\]
Thus the \(p\)-adic valuation of \(\prod_{k<r}d_k(n)\) is at most the valuation of \(Ka(n)\). Since (21) holds for every prime \(p\), divisibility (13) follows.

## 5. Returning to the signed product

The absolute value of the signed denominator product is
\[
|D_r(n)|
=
\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}|8n-(2k+1)|
=
\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}d_k(n).
\]
By (13), this positive integer divides \(K(r)a(n)\). Divisibility by an integer and by its absolute value are equivalent, so
\[
D_r(n)\mid K(r)a(n)
\]
in \(\mathbb Z\).

Finally, the integer
\[
K(r)=\left(\bigl(3(2r+1)\bigr)!\right)^r
\]
is positive. This also covers \(r=0\), when the empty product is \(1\) and \(K(0)=1\). Therefore, for every nonnegative integer \(r\), there is a positive integer \(K(r)\) such that
\[
\prod_{k=0}^{r-1}(8n-(2k+1))\mid K(r)a(n)
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(n\), as required.
